summary: Describes SIV (Synthetic Initialization Vector), a block cipher mode of operation. It takes a key, a plaintext, and multiple variable-length strings that are authenticated but not encrypted, and produces ciphertext of the same length plus a synthetic initialization vector. Depending on use, it gives deterministic authenticated encryption or protection against misuse of nonces.

plainLanguage.summary: SIV creates an authentication value from the plaintext and associated data, then uses it to encrypt the plaintext. If a nonce is reused, the message remains authenticated, but repeated inputs can be recognized.

questions: how does siv handle nonce reuse
subtitle: An AES mode for authenticated encryption that can also tolerate nonce reuse

tldr.problem: Many authenticated-encryption modes depend on unique nonces, and accidental nonce reuse can seriously weaken security.
tldr.mechanism: SIV uses S2V with AES-CMAC to create a synthetic initialization vector, then AES counter mode to encrypt the plaintext.
tldr.outcome: SIV supports nonce-based authenticated encryption and deterministic key wrapping. Reusing a nonce preserves authenticity but reveals when the same plaintext and associated data recur.

today: RFC 5297 is an Informational description of the SIV-AES mode, published in October 2008. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SIV Was Designed
sections.content:
Nonce-based authenticated encryption generally requires a nonce not to repeat with the same key. An application can accidentally reuse one because of faulty randomness, reset state, or a virtual-machine rollback.

RFC 5297 describes SIV as a mode for both nonce-based encryption and deterministic key wrapping. It also accepts multiple associated-data strings, which are authenticated but not encrypted.
sections.plainLanguage: Some encryption methods become unsafe if an application repeats a nonce. SIV is designed to retain authenticity if that mistake occurs.

sections.title: S2V and Counter-Mode Encryption
sections.content:
SIV splits its key into two equal parts. S2V uses AES-CMAC to process the associated data and plaintext and produce a 128-bit synthetic initialization vector.

AES counter mode uses that value to encrypt the plaintext. The result contains the synthetic vector followed by ciphertext whose length matches the plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: One part of SIV computes a check value from the data. The other part uses that value to encrypt the data.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
To encrypt, SIV runs S2V on the associated-data strings and plaintext, then uses the resulting vector as the starting counter for AES counter mode. The output includes the 128-bit vector and the encrypted plaintext.

To decrypt, the receiver uses the vector to recover the plaintext and runs S2V again with the same associated data. It returns the plaintext only if the newly computed vector matches the received one; otherwise, it returns FAIL.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver decrypts the data and recomputes its check value. If the values differ, the receiver rejects the message.

sections.title: Nonce-Based and Deterministic Uses
sections.content:
For nonce-based encryption, the nonce is one associated-data component. When it does not repeat with the same key, SIV provides the usual nonce-based authenticated-encryption behavior. If it repeats, authenticity remains, but an observer can learn that the same plaintext and associated data were protected with that nonce and key.

For deterministic authenticated encryption, SIV can wrap unpredictable data such as a cryptographic key without a nonce. Encrypting the same input with the same associated data produces the same output.
sections.plainLanguage: SIV can use a nonce for ordinary authenticated encryption or omit it when wrapping unpredictable data. Reusing a nonce can reveal repeated inputs, but does not remove the authenticity check.

sections.title: Limits and Performance
sections.content:
SIV makes two passes over the data: one to compute S2V and one to encrypt with counter mode. The RFC notes that this can be slower than modes designed for higher throughput.

The security analysis limits S2V to 127 total input components, including the plaintext, so SIV can safely take at most 126 associated-data components. The RFC also recommends limiting distinct invocations under one key to 2^48.
sections.plainLanguage: SIV uses extra processing to provide resistance to nonce mistakes. Its security analysis also limits how many associated-data components and key uses should be allowed.
